bull_bear.body:
- Fully integrated manufacturing - pulp production, paper manufacturing, captive power generation and a chemical recovery system - which sustained a competitive cost structure amid changing market conditions
- Scale with near-full asset utilisation: the Dandeli mill ran at around 99.98% capacity utilisation in FY 2025-26, giving economies of scale
- Established distribution: 72 long-standing dealers and six zonal offices, with exports to more than 15 countries
- Long-standing brand and presence since 1955 in India's writing and printing paper segment, marketing under the WESCO brand including customised security papers for banks
- Raw material security via 75% local pulpwood sourcing from Karnataka (supplemented by Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra), a defined agro-forestry and farm forestry promotion programme with site-specific clones, demonstration plots and partner nurseries
- Backward integration in cables - the greenfield optical fibre plant at Fab City, Hyderabad ensures a reliable supply of optical fibre, a key raw material for the Mysore and Hyderabad cable plants
- R&D and application engineering teams supporting portfolio expansion into telecom and utility segments, with ongoing development of products aligned to 5G and data centre requirements
- Growing export acceptance in cables - optical fibre and optical fibre cables exported to more than 25 countries
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Pulpwood / wood availability and cost — The BRSR material-issues table identifies wood as the primary raw material for pulp manufacturing and states that 'securing a sustained supply of high-quality wood remains a critical challenge', with the financial implication flagged as negative: 'Shortage of wood may lead to high cost of sourcing of wood'. This is not theoretical - the Directors' Report attributes the FY 2025-26 earnings decline partly to an increase in wood cost. Mitigation rests on an agro-forestry and farm-forestry promotion programme, site-specific clones, demonstration plots, partner nurseries, inter-state procurement and imported wood chips, all of which are multi-year in effect.
- Low-priced imports and realisation pressure — The Directors' Report states performance 'got impacted compared to the previous year primarily lower realization caused by surge in low priced imports'. The Chairman echoes this, citing pressure from low-priced imports, volatile raw material costs and softer realisations. The MD&A adds that industry margins were pressured by elevated raw material costs, competition from low-priced imports and GST-related disruptions, and lists import pressure among the challenges the industry must still navigate; the Minimum Import Price on paperboard is described as a policy buffer, which makes the risk policy-dependent.
- Structural decline in writing and printing paper from digitisation — West Coast Paper's core product line is writing and printing paper, but the MD&A records that the global writing and printing segment declined 0-1% and 'is expected to contract further on the back of accelerating digitisation', with newsprint down 1-3% as e-paper readership expanded. Growth in the industry is concentrated in packaging, hygiene and specialty grades, so the Company's exposure depends on how fast it can shift its mix toward value-added and speciality products.
- Industry cyclicality and capacity additions — The AR describes the Indian paper industry as operating 'in a cyclical environment, with performance closely linked to overall economic conditions, input costs, and demand trends across packaging, education, and industrial sectors', and notes the industry is fragmented (around 526 mills) with capacity additions of approximately 1.8-2.2 Million Tonnes underway. New supply against 6-8% projected demand growth is a structural pricing risk, particularly for a plant already running at 99.98% utilisation with no volume lever left.
- Energy cost and efficiency / BEE compliance — The BRSR material-issues table flags energy management as both risk and opportunity: 'With increasing scarcity of natural resources and increasing cost, efficient management of energy becomes critical for uninterrupted business operations', with negative implications stated as 'Increases the cost of production and may not meet target set by BEE requirement'. Paper is energy-intensive and the mill relies on 74.8 MW of captive generation, so energy economics feed directly into the cost structure.
- Environmental compliance - water, air emissions and effluent — The BRSR flags environment management as a risk: 'As Water is a critical operational input, we have to strictly monitor our processes to ensure full compliance with all regulatory standards for air emissions, water consumption, and effluent discharge.' Compliance with stringent environmental regulations is described elsewhere in the AR as requiring significant capital investment, and the Company has had to deploy CEMS, online effluent monitoring, upgraded tertiary treatment for pulp effluent and enhanced secondary treatment for paper machine effluent. An integrated pulp mill's licence to operate is contingent on this.
- Product quality and brand reputation — The first material issue in the BRSR table is product quality: 'Any lapse in product quality would negatively impact our brand value and market share.' This matters disproportionately for West Coast Paper because a chunk of its premium positioning rests on trust-dependent grades - customised, watermarked security paper used by banks to print cheque leaves, and premium printing papers under the WESCO brand - where a quality failure would cost the customer relationship, not just a batch.
- Telecom capex cyclicality and competition in the optical fibre cable business — The cable division, now the Company's declared growth avenue and the destination of the Hyderabad capex, is exposed to sectoral threats the AR itself lists: competition from domestic and global OFC manufacturers, alternative wireless technologies for last-mile connectivity that could reduce fibre dependence and pressure pricing, geopolitical and supply-chain disruption in critical inputs such as optical fibre preforms and specialty materials, and telecom capex cyclicality - 'Any slowdown or deferment in telecom investments, including delays in 5G rollout or broadband expansion, could temporarily affect order inflows.' Demand is also visibly policy-linked, through BharatNet allocations and domestic-supply preference. OFC sales volume already fell about 1% in FY 2025-26 on volatile market conditions.
- Human resource and human rights governance — The BRSR flags that the absence of a comprehensive human rights governance structure covering working conditions, child/forced labour, fair remuneration, gender diversity, prevention of sexual harassment and freedom of association 'will adversely impact the Company's smooth working & people development'. The workforce is also heavily contract-weighted - 2,383 of 3,869 workers are other than permanent - and permanent-employee turnover rose to 9.31% in FY 2025-26 from 8.50% and 6.46% in the two prior years, a three-year uptrend in attrition.

business.body: West Coast Paper Mills manufactures and markets writing, printing and value-added paper and paperboard under the WESCO brand from a fully integrated mill at Dandeli, Karnataka that combines pulp production, paper manufacturing, captive power generation and a chemical recovery system. Its cable division, West Coast Optilinks (formerly Sudarshan Telecom, founded 1996), manufactures optical fibre cables at Mysore and Hyderabad and, following commissioning of an optical fibre plant at Fab City, Hyderabad, now also makes optical fibre for backward integration. Products are sold across India through a long-standing dealer network and to the Indian telecom and utilities sectors, with exports to Europe and the MEA region.

outlook.body:
- Build a diversified, future-oriented business portfolio beyond the traditional boundaries of the paper industry, with optical fibre and cable positioned as the strategic growth avenue alongside paper and paperboard as the core foundation.
- Continue phase-wise investment at the Paper Division, Dandeli aimed at improving paper quality, producing new speciality products, and reducing consumption of steam, power, chemicals and water while minimising machine breakdowns.
- Expand the Cable Division's product portfolio to consolidate its position in the Indian market and grow international business.
- Improve operating efficiencies through a better product mix, in response to lower realisations caused by low-priced imports and higher wood cost.
- Deepen backward integration in the fibre value chain - the optical fibre plant at Fab City, Hyderabad secures supply for the Mysore and Hyderabad cable plants and increases participation in a value chain critical to 5G, digital connectivity and data infrastructure.
- Strengthen the value-added / speciality paper portfolio, evidenced by new products introduced during the year (Xellent Pro Shrink Wrap, Wesco Stylo Coat, Wesco Dura Board) and by the WESCO brand serving applications from premium printing papers to customised security papers for banks.
- Use technology to raise productivity and resource efficiency - disc filters for improved fibre recovery, upgrades to key machine components, energy-efficient systems and optimisation of steam and power utilisation.
- Sustain a raw-material security strategy through the plantation and farm forestry programme, with over 200 lakh seedlings and saplings planted during FY 2025-26.
- Reduce fossil fuel dependence through increased use of biomass and chemical recovery systems, alongside water conservation, recycling and energy efficiency initiatives.
- Maintain a balanced capital allocation approach - rewarding shareholders through dividend while preserving financial strength to support future growth and strategic investments.

outlook.body: West Coast Paper Mills' expansion narrative in FY 2025-26 centres on the optical fibre value chain at Fab City, Hyderabad, Telangana. West Coast Optilinks (the cable division, formerly Sudarshan Telecom) had already expanded its production footprint by commissioning a new optical fibre cable manufacturing unit there in response to global demand driven by 5G deployments, effectively doubling its optical fibre cable capacity, with commercial operations commencing on 14 February 2024. During FY 2025-26 the Company took the next step in that programme: the greenfield Optical Fibre manufacturing plant set up at the same Fab City location became operational, strengthening backward integration and ensuring a stable supply of optical fibre - a key raw material - for both the Mysore and Hyderabad cable plants. In its first year of operation the new fibre plant recorded production of 26.50 lakh FKM (26,50,270 FKM) against Nil in the prior year, with sales of 8.14 lakh FKM. The Company describes this as aligning with its long-term strategic vision and with national initiatives such as Atmanirbhar Bharat and Digital India, and the Chairman calls the Hyderabad expansion 'another important milestone', noting that the new cable facility enhanced installed capacity while the fibre plant improved supply reliability, together creating a more integrated and future-ready platform for domestic and international markets. On the paper side there is no new greenfield project; the stated FUTURE PLAN is continuous phase-wise investment at the Paper Division, Dandeli aimed at improving paper quality, producing new speciality products and reducing usage of steam, power, chemicals and water while minimising machine breakdowns. Specific FY 2025-26 paper-division works cited include the PM-1 Disc Filter, the Recovery Island Press Filter, disc filters for improved fibre recovery, upgrades to key machine components, energy-efficient systems and optimisation of steam and power utilisation - described as 'Continuous Modernization for Efficiency, Sustainability and Reliability'. The Dandeli mill ran at 99.98% capacity utilisation, leaving little headroom without further debottlenecking. The Cable Division is separately expanding its product portfolio to consolidate its Indian market position and grow international business.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Indian domestic paper and paperboard demand is estimated to have grown 5-7% in FY 2025-26, led by healthy offtake from FMCG, e-commerce and pharmaceutical end-use industries; demand growth is projected at 6-8% over FY 2026-27.
- India is the third-largest consumer of paper and paperboard globally at around 23-24 Million Tonnes annually, with per capita consumption of only about 15 kg against a global average of 57 kg - management cites significant headroom for long-term expansion.
- Packaging paper and paperboard account for nearly 65% of Indian volumes and are the backbone of the market; specialty paper including tissue and thermal paper is expected to grow at an 11-13% CAGR.
- Globally the writing and printing segment declined 0-1% and is expected to contract further on accelerating digitisation, while global paperboard grew 2-4% and is expected to be the principal long-term demand driver.
- Margin pressure from elevated raw material costs, competition from low-priced imports and GST-related disruptions - the Company's own FY 2025-26 performance was hit by lower realisation from a surge in low-priced imports and an increase in wood cost.
- Global pulp prices firmed during the period, with softwood and hardwood pulp up approximately 7% and 8% respectively, though realisations are expected to remain broadly range-bound over the longer term.
- Policy support for paper: the ban on single-use plastics and the New Education Policy (NEP 2020) provide structural demand support, while the Minimum Import Price on paperboard acts as a key policy buffer.
- Industry supply: capacity additions of approximately 1.8-2.2 Million Tonnes are underway in India, and the domestic industry remains fragmented with roughly 526 mills.
- Indian raw material constraint - limited domestic availability, wastepaper recovery of only about 30%, forcing industry players to import pulp, wastepaper and pulpwood at premium cost.
- The Indian optical fibre cable sector recovered during FY 2025-26 after several subdued quarters, driven by 5G fronthaul and backhaul rollouts, the BharatNet Phase III rural broadband programme, hyperscale data centre expansion and rising export orders.
- Tariff and non-tariff barriers on Chinese optical cable imports tightened and government preference for domestic supply in BharatNet and 5G procurement reinforced the position of Indian manufacturers; the India fibre optics market is projected to grow at a 10-14% CAGR over the medium term, supported by Digital India and the Smart Cities Mission.
- The global fibre optic cable market (US$ 12.5-13.8 Billion) is projected to expand at roughly 10% CAGR through the next decade on 5G standalone rollouts, hyperscale data centre bandwidth needs for AI computing and national FTTH broadband initiatives.
- Union Budget FY 2026-27 as a demand signal: total telecom outlay raised nearly 38% to Rs 73,990 Crore, BharatNet allocation raised to Rs 20,000 Crore from a revised Rs 5,500 Crore, Rs 2,098 Crore for fibre/4G/5G/satellite connectivity in the North-East and Rs 975 Crore for a defence optical fibre network - expected to underpin domestic OFC demand through FY 2026-27.
- Union Budget infrastructure spending raised about 11% to a record Rs 12.2 Lakh Crore, expected to drive demand for industrial paper, packaging board and telecom infrastructure including optical fibre deployment; continued income tax relief supports consumption and packaging demand.
- Management's own outlook: a diversified business portfolio, strong manufacturing base, trusted brand equity and operational excellence are described as a solid foundation for long-term growth, with the Hyderabad expansion creating a more integrated platform for both domestic and international markets.

currentContext.expansion: West Coast Paper Mills' expansion narrative in FY 2025-26 centres on the optical fibre value chain at Fab City, Hyderabad, Telangana. West Coast Optilinks (the cable division, formerly Sudarshan Telecom) had already expanded its production footprint by commissioning a new optical fibre cable manufacturing unit there in response to global demand driven by 5G deployments, effectively doubling its optical fibre cable capacity, with commercial operations commencing on 14 February 2024. During FY 2025-26 the Company took the next step in that programme: the greenfield Optical Fibre manufacturing plant set up at the same Fab City location became operational, strengthening backward integration and ensuring a stable supply of optical fibre - a key raw material - for both the Mysore and Hyderabad cable plants. In its first year of operation the new fibre plant recorded production of 26.50 lakh FKM (26,50,270 FKM) against Nil in the prior year, with sales of 8.14 lakh FKM. The Company describes this as aligning with its long-term strategic vision and with national initiatives such as Atmanirbhar Bharat and Digital India, and the Chairman calls the Hyderabad expansion 'another important milestone', noting that the new cable facility enhanced installed capacity while the fibre plant improved supply reliability, together creating a more integrated and future-ready platform for domestic and international markets. On the paper side there is no new greenfield project; the stated FUTURE PLAN is continuous phase-wise investment at the Paper Division, Dandeli aimed at improving paper quality, producing new speciality products and reducing usage of steam, power, chemicals and water while minimising machine breakdowns. Specific FY 2025-26 paper-division works cited include the PM-1 Disc Filter, the Recovery Island Press Filter, disc filters for improved fibre recovery, upgrades to key machine components, energy-efficient systems and optimisation of steam and power utilisation - described as 'Continuous Modernization for Efficiency, Sustainability and Reliability'. The Dandeli mill ran at 99.98% capacity utilisation, leaving little headroom without further debottlenecking. The Cable Division is separately expanding its product portfolio to consolidate its Indian market position and grow international business.

risks.note: The BRSR material-issues table identifies wood as the primary raw material for pulp manufacturing and states that 'securing a sustained supply of high-quality wood remains a critical challenge', with the financial implication flagged as negative: 'Shortage of wood may lead to high cost of sourcing of wood'. This is not theoretical - the Directors' Report attributes the FY 2025-26 earnings decline partly to an increase in wood cost. Mitigation rests on an agro-forestry and farm-forestry promotion programme, site-specific clones, demonstration plots, partner nurseries, inter-state procurement and imported wood chips, all of which are multi-year in effect.

The Directors' Report states performance 'got impacted compared to the previous year primarily lower realization caused by surge in low priced imports'. The Chairman echoes this, citing pressure from low-priced imports, volatile raw material costs and softer realisations. The MD&A adds that industry margins were pressured by elevated raw material costs, competition from low-priced imports and GST-related disruptions, and lists import pressure among the challenges the industry must still navigate; the Minimum Import Price on paperboard is described as a policy buffer, which makes the risk policy-dependent.

risks.risk: Structural decline in writing and printing paper from digitisation
risks.note: West Coast Paper's core product line is writing and printing paper, but the MD&A records that the global writing and printing segment declined 0-1% and 'is expected to contract further on the back of accelerating digitisation', with newsprint down 1-3% as e-paper readership expanded. Growth in the industry is concentrated in packaging, hygiene and specialty grades, so the Company's exposure depends on how fast it can shift its mix toward value-added and speciality products.

The AR describes the Indian paper industry as operating 'in a cyclical environment, with performance closely linked to overall economic conditions, input costs, and demand trends across packaging, education, and industrial sectors', and notes the industry is fragmented (around 526 mills) with capacity additions of approximately 1.8-2.2 Million Tonnes underway. New supply against 6-8% projected demand growth is a structural pricing risk, particularly for a plant already running at 99.98% utilisation with no volume lever left.

risks.risk: Energy cost and efficiency / BEE compliance
risks.note: The BRSR material-issues table flags energy management as both risk and opportunity: 'With increasing scarcity of natural resources and increasing cost, efficient management of energy becomes critical for uninterrupted business operations', with negative implications stated as 'Increases the cost of production and may not meet target set by BEE requirement'. Paper is energy-intensive and the mill relies on 74.8 MW of captive generation, so energy economics feed directly into the cost structure.

risks.risk: Environmental compliance - water, air emissions and effluent
risks.note: The BRSR flags environment management as a risk: 'As Water is a critical operational input, we have to strictly monitor our processes to ensure full compliance with all regulatory standards for air emissions, water consumption, and effluent discharge.' Compliance with stringent environmental regulations is described elsewhere in the AR as requiring significant capital investment, and the Company has had to deploy CEMS, online effluent monitoring, upgraded tertiary treatment for pulp effluent and enhanced secondary treatment for paper machine effluent. An integrated pulp mill's licence to operate is contingent on this.

The first material issue in the BRSR table is product quality: 'Any lapse in product quality would negatively impact our brand value and market share.' This matters disproportionately for West Coast Paper because a chunk of its premium positioning rests on trust-dependent grades - customised, watermarked security paper used by banks to print cheque leaves, and premium printing papers under the WESCO brand - where a quality failure would cost the customer relationship, not just a batch.

risks.risk: Telecom capex cyclicality and competition in the optical fibre cable business
risks.note: The cable division, now the Company's declared growth avenue and the destination of the Hyderabad capex, is exposed to sectoral threats the AR itself lists: competition from domestic and global OFC manufacturers, alternative wireless technologies for last-mile connectivity that could reduce fibre dependence and pressure pricing, geopolitical and supply-chain disruption in critical inputs such as optical fibre preforms and specialty materials, and telecom capex cyclicality - 'Any slowdown or deferment in telecom investments, including delays in 5G rollout or broadband expansion, could temporarily affect order inflows.' Demand is also visibly policy-linked, through BharatNet allocations and domestic-supply preference. OFC sales volume already fell about 1% in FY 2025-26 on volatile market conditions.

risks.risk: Human resource and human rights governance
risks.note: The BRSR flags that the absence of a comprehensive human rights governance structure covering working conditions, child/forced labour, fair remuneration, gender diversity, prevention of sexual harassment and freedom of association 'will adversely impact the Company's smooth working & people development'. The workforce is also heavily contract-weighted - 2,383 of 3,869 workers are other than permanent - and permanent-employee turnover rose to 9.31% in FY 2025-26 from 8.50% and 6.46% in the two prior years, a three-year uptrend in attrition.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Established in 1955 and the flagship company of the SK Bangur Group, West Coast Paper Mills is a prominent player in India's writing and printing paper segment, operating a fully integrated 320,000 MTPA paper mill at Dandeli, Karnataka alongside a growing optical fibre and cable business.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: West Coast Paper Mills manufactures and markets writing, printing and value-added paper and paperboard under the WESCO brand from a fully integrated mill at Dandeli, Karnataka that combines pulp production, paper manufacturing, captive power generation and a chemical recovery system. Its cable division, West Coast Optilinks (formerly Sudarshan Telecom, founded 1996), manufactures optical fibre cables at Mysore and Hyderabad and, following commissioning of an optical fibre plant at Fab City, Hyderabad, now also makes optical fibre for backward integration. Products are sold across India through a long-standing dealer network and to the Indian telecom and utilities sectors, with exports to Europe and the MEA region.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian domestic paper and paperboard demand is estimated to have grown 5-7% in FY 2025-26, led by healthy offtake from FMCG, e-commerce and pharmaceutical end-use industries; demand growth is projected at 6-8% over FY 2026-27.
- India is the third-largest consumer of paper and paperboard globally at around 23-24 Million Tonnes annually, with per capita consumption of only about 15 kg against a global average of 57 kg - management cites significant headroom for long-term expansion.
- Packaging paper and paperboard account for nearly 65% of Indian volumes and are the backbone of the market; specialty paper including tissue and thermal paper is expected to grow at an 11-13% CAGR.
- Globally the writing and printing segment declined 0-1% and is expected to contract further on accelerating digitisation, while global paperboard grew 2-4% and is expected to be the principal long-term demand driver.
- Margin pressure from elevated raw material costs, competition from low-priced imports and GST-related disruptions - the Company's own FY 2025-26 performance was hit by lower realisation from a surge in low-priced imports and an increase in wood cost.
- Global pulp prices firmed during the period, with softwood and hardwood pulp up approximately 7% and 8% respectively, though realisations are expected to remain broadly range-bound over the longer term.
- Policy support for paper: the ban on single-use plastics and the New Education Policy (NEP 2020) provide structural demand support, while the Minimum Import Price on paperboard acts as a key policy buffer.
- Industry supply: capacity additions of approximately 1.8-2.2 Million Tonnes are underway in India, and the domestic industry remains fragmented with roughly 526 mills.
- Indian raw material constraint - limited domestic availability, wastepaper recovery of only about 30%, forcing industry players to import pulp, wastepaper and pulpwood at premium cost.
- The Indian optical fibre cable sector recovered during FY 2025-26 after several subdued quarters, driven by 5G fronthaul and backhaul rollouts, the BharatNet Phase III rural broadband programme, hyperscale data centre expansion and rising export orders.
- Tariff and non-tariff barriers on Chinese optical cable imports tightened and government preference for domestic supply in BharatNet and 5G procurement reinforced the position of Indian manufacturers; the India fibre optics market is projected to grow at a 10-14% CAGR over the medium term, supported by Digital India and the Smart Cities Mission.
- The global fibre optic cable market (US$ 12.5-13.8 Billion) is projected to expand at roughly 10% CAGR through the next decade on 5G standalone rollouts, hyperscale data centre bandwidth needs for AI computing and national FTTH broadband initiatives.
- Union Budget FY 2026-27 as a demand signal: total telecom outlay raised nearly 38% to Rs 73,990 Crore, BharatNet allocation raised to Rs 20,000 Crore from a revised Rs 5,500 Crore, Rs 2,098 Crore for fibre/4G/5G/satellite connectivity in the North-East and Rs 975 Crore for a defence optical fibre network - expected to underpin domestic OFC demand through FY 2026-27.
- Union Budget infrastructure spending raised about 11% to a record Rs 12.2 Lakh Crore, expected to drive demand for industrial paper, packaging board and telecom infrastructure including optical fibre deployment; continued income tax relief supports consumption and packaging demand.
- Management's own outlook: a diversified business portfolio, strong manufacturing base, trusted brand equity and operational excellence are described as a solid foundation for long-term growth, with the Hyderabad expansion creating a more integrated platform for both domestic and international markets.

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Build a diversified, future-oriented business portfolio beyond the traditional boundaries of the paper industry, with optical fibre and cable positioned as the strategic growth avenue alongside paper and paperboard as the core foundation.
- Continue phase-wise investment at the Paper Division, Dandeli aimed at improving paper quality, producing new speciality products, and reducing consumption of steam, power, chemicals and water while minimising machine breakdowns.
- Expand the Cable Division's product portfolio to consolidate its position in the Indian market and grow international business.
- Improve operating efficiencies through a better product mix, in response to lower realisations caused by low-priced imports and higher wood cost.
- Deepen backward integration in the fibre value chain - the optical fibre plant at Fab City, Hyderabad secures supply for the Mysore and Hyderabad cable plants and increases participation in a value chain critical to 5G, digital connectivity and data infrastructure.
- Strengthen the value-added / speciality paper portfolio, evidenced by new products introduced during the year (Xellent Pro Shrink Wrap, Wesco Stylo Coat, Wesco Dura Board) and by the WESCO brand serving applications from premium printing papers to customised security papers for banks.
- Use technology to raise productivity and resource efficiency - disc filters for improved fibre recovery, upgrades to key machine components, energy-efficient systems and optimisation of steam and power utilisation.
- Sustain a raw-material security strategy through the plantation and farm forestry programme, with over 200 lakh seedlings and saplings planted during FY 2025-26.
- Reduce fossil fuel dependence through increased use of biomass and chemical recovery systems, alongside water conservation, recycling and energy efficiency initiatives.
- Maintain a balanced capital allocation approach - rewarding shareholders through dividend while preserving financial strength to support future growth and strategic investments.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: West Coast Paper Mills' expansion narrative in FY 2025-26 centres on the optical fibre value chain at Fab City, Hyderabad, Telangana. West Coast Optilinks (the cable division, formerly Sudarshan Telecom) had already expanded its production footprint by commissioning a new optical fibre cable manufacturing unit there in response to global demand driven by 5G deployments, effectively doubling its optical fibre cable capacity, with commercial operations commencing on 14 February 2024. During FY 2025-26 the Company took the next step in that programme: the greenfield Optical Fibre manufacturing plant set up at the same Fab City location became operational, strengthening backward integration and ensuring a stable supply of optical fibre - a key raw material - for both the Mysore and Hyderabad cable plants. In its first year of operation the new fibre plant recorded production of 26.50 lakh FKM (26,50,270 FKM) against Nil in the prior year, with sales of 8.14 lakh FKM. The Company describes this as aligning with its long-term strategic vision and with national initiatives such as Atmanirbhar Bharat and Digital India, and the Chairman calls the Hyderabad expansion 'another important milestone', noting that the new cable facility enhanced installed capacity while the fibre plant improved supply reliability, together creating a more integrated and future-ready platform for domestic and international markets. On the paper side there is no new greenfield project; the stated FUTURE PLAN is continuous phase-wise investment at the Paper Division, Dandeli aimed at improving paper quality, producing new speciality products and reducing usage of steam, power, chemicals and water while minimising machine breakdowns. Specific FY 2025-26 paper-division works cited include the PM-1 Disc Filter, the Recovery Island Press Filter, disc filters for improved fibre recovery, upgrades to key machine components, energy-efficient systems and optimisation of steam and power utilisation - described as 'Continuous Modernization for Efficiency, Sustainability and Reliability'. The Dandeli mill ran at 99.98% capacity utilisation, leaving little headroom without further debottlenecking. The Cable Division is separately expanding its product portfolio to consolidate its Indian market position and grow international business.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Fully integrated manufacturing - pulp production, paper manufacturing, captive power generation and a chemical recovery system - which sustained a competitive cost structure amid changing market conditions
- Scale with near-full asset utilisation: the Dandeli mill ran at around 99.98% capacity utilisation in FY 2025-26, giving economies of scale
- Established distribution: 72 long-standing dealers and six zonal offices, with exports to more than 15 countries
- Long-standing brand and presence since 1955 in India's writing and printing paper segment, marketing under the WESCO brand including customised security papers for banks

- Backward integration in cables - the greenfield optical fibre plant at Fab City, Hyderabad ensures a reliable supply of optical fibre, a key raw material for the Mysore and Hyderabad cable plants
- R&D and application engineering teams supporting portfolio expansion into telecom and utility segments, with ongoing development of products aligned to 5G and data centre requirements
- Growing export acceptance in cables - optical fibre and optical fibre cables exported to more than 25 countries

This is not theoretical - the Directors' Report attributes the FY 2025-26 earnings decline partly to an increase in wood cost. Mitigation rests on an agro-forestry and farm-forestry promotion programme, site-specific clones, demonstration plots, partner nurseries, inter-state procurement and imported wood chips, all of which are multi-year in effect.
- Low-priced imports and realisation pressure — The Directors' Report states performance 'got impacted compared to the previous year primarily lower realization caused by surge in low priced imports'. The Chairman echoes this, citing pressure from low-priced imports, volatile raw material costs and softer realisations. The MD&A adds that industry margins were pressured by elevated raw material costs, competition from low-priced imports and GST-related disruptions, and lists import pressure among the challenges the industry must still navigate; the Minimum Import Price on paperboard is described as a policy buffer, which makes the risk policy-dependent.
- Structural decline in writing and printing paper from digitisation — West Coast Paper's core product line is writing and printing paper, but the MD&A records that the global writing and printing segment declined 0-1% and 'is expected to contract further on the back of accelerating digitisation', with newsprint down 1-3% as e-paper readership expanded. Growth in the industry is concentrated in packaging, hygiene and specialty grades, so the Company's exposure depends on how fast it can shift its mix toward value-added and speciality products.
- Industry cyclicality and capacity additions — The AR describes the Indian paper industry as operating 'in a cyclical environment, with performance closely linked to overall economic conditions, input costs, and demand trends across packaging, education, and industrial sectors', and notes the industry is fragmented (around 526 mills) with capacity additions of approximately 1.8-2.2 Million Tonnes underway. New supply against 6-8% projected demand growth is a structural pricing risk, particularly for a plant already running at 99.98% utilisation with no volume lever left.
- Energy cost and efficiency / BEE compliance — The BRSR material-issues table flags energy management as both risk and opportunity: 'With increasing scarcity of natural resources and increasing cost, efficient management of energy becomes critical for uninterrupted business operations', with negative implications stated as 'Increases the cost of production and may not meet target set by BEE requirement'. Paper is energy-intensive and the mill relies on 74.8 MW of captive generation, so energy economics feed directly into the cost structure.
- Environmental compliance - water, air emissions and effluent — The BRSR flags environment management as a risk: 'As Water is a critical operational input, we have to strictly monitor our processes to ensure full compliance with all regulatory standards for air emissions, water consumption, and effluent discharge.' Compliance with stringent environmental regulations is described elsewhere in the AR as requiring significant capital investment, and the Company has had to deploy CEMS, online effluent monitoring, upgraded tertiary treatment for pulp effluent and enhanced secondary treatment for paper machine effluent. An integrated pulp mill's licence to operate is contingent on this.
- Product quality and brand reputation — The first material issue in the BRSR table is product quality: 'Any lapse in product quality would negatively impact our brand value and market share.' This matters disproportionately for West Coast Paper because a chunk of its premium positioning rests on trust-dependent grades - customised, watermarked security paper used by banks to print cheque leaves, and premium printing papers under the WESCO brand - where a quality failure would cost the customer relationship, not just a batch.
- Telecom capex cyclicality and competition in the optical fibre cable business — The cable division, now the Company's declared growth avenue and the destination of the Hyderabad capex, is exposed to sectoral threats the AR itself lists: competition from domestic and global OFC manufacturers, alternative wireless technologies for last-mile connectivity that could reduce fibre dependence and pressure pricing, geopolitical and supply-chain disruption in critical inputs such as optical fibre preforms and specialty materials, and telecom capex cyclicality - 'Any slowdown or deferment in telecom investments, including delays in 5G rollout or broadband expansion, could temporarily affect order inflows.' Demand is also visibly policy-linked, through BharatNet allocations and domestic-supply preference. OFC sales volume already fell about 1% in FY 2025-26 on volatile market conditions.
- Human resource and human rights governance — The BRSR flags that the absence of a comprehensive human rights governance structure covering working conditions, child/forced labour, fair remuneration, gender diversity, prevention of sexual harassment and freedom of association 'will adversely impact the Company's smooth working & people development'. The workforce is also heavily contract-weighted - 2,383 of 3,869 workers are other than permanent - and permanent-employee turnover rose to 9.31% in FY 2025-26 from 8.50% and 6.46% in the two prior years, a three-year uptrend in attrition.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Build a diversified, future-oriented business portfolio beyond the traditional boundaries of the paper industry, with optical fibre and cable positioned as the strategic growth avenue alongside paper and paperboard as the core foundation.
- Continue phase-wise investment at the Paper Division, Dandeli aimed at improving paper quality, producing new speciality products, and reducing consumption of steam, power, chemicals and water while minimising machine breakdowns.
- Expand the Cable Division's product portfolio to consolidate its position in the Indian market and grow international …

hero.oneLiner: Established in 1955 and the flagship company of the SK Bangur Group, West Coast Paper Mills is a prominent player in India's writing and printing paper segment, operating a fully integrated 320,000 MTPA paper mill at Dandeli, Karnataka alongside a growing optical fibre and cable business.
